lane_claim:
**Residual, stated rather than hidden.** The barrier works at microtask granularity, so a gate
that closes during the confirming pass, inside the same drain as a hold that answers late, can
still let the request out. No bounded number of passes closes that for holds that always answer
late; the alternative is an unbounded loop, which hangs on a hold that parks on every call. It is
documented at `holdAllBeforeDispatch`.
falsifying_evidence:
1. `AgentPauseGate.dispatchHold(signal, next)` checks the process gate, then waits for `next`. Close the process gate while `next` waits for an entire event-loop turn, then resolve `next`: the request sends under the closed gate. This is **not** the declared microtask residual.

```text
NESTED_HOLD_REPAUSE { sent: [true], paused: true }
```

2. With two independent wrapper layers, have the second hold answer asynchronously and close the first gate during its second/confirming pass:

```text
CONFIRMING_MICROTASK { sent: [true], lateCalls: 2, calls: ["b", "a"] }
```

The return at `dispatch-hold.ts:84` accepts an answer it knows was asynchronous without revalidating the earlier gate. Calling this a barrier does not make the admitted request safe. The reported residual is reproducible and violates the hard dispatch contract.

lane_claim:
A transport that carries a caller's wrapper is per-request state, so it is live: a hold supplied
later is added to that build and the same fetch comes back, and a wrapper supplied later is
layered outside it, in the order a rebuild would have used. A stamped fetch with no wrapper is
still rebuilt as before. `withoutDispatchHold` never hands back a live build as its own unheld
transport, even while that build has no hold, because a hold joining later would otherwise gate
cleanup traffic too.
falsifying_evidence:
```text
UNHELD_WRAPPER_REBUILD { builds: 2, wires: 2 }
```

A one-attempt wrapper that had already spent its budget gets a fresh counter on the unheld derivative.

lane_claim:
**Prewarm — decision.** The reviewer's `PREWARM` probe still passes, and that is deliberate: it
calls `prewarmModelConnection` and `prewarmOpenAICodexResponses` directly, and `packages/ai`
cannot see a host's pause gate. Every in-product caller is covered instead — the five `sdk.ts`
sites and `AgentSession.prewarmModelConnection` (which the interactive mode and the input
controller call) go through `prewarmUnlessPaused`, which skips while paused.
falsifying_evidence:
Call the actual in-product `prewarmUnlessPaused`, pause while request-debug preparation is awaiting, then release preparation:

```text
PRODUCT_HTTP_PREWARM_RACE { seen: [{method:"HEAD", paused:true}] }
0 pass / 1 fail
```

The new caller guard prevents a prewarm **started** while paused; it does not prevent one **dispatched** while paused. It passes no final hold into `transportFetch`.

lane_claim:
**Decisions.** (a) Held time is excluded by restarting the watchdog's budget when the hold ends,
so wire-to-first-event still has exactly one budget; the provider-only alternative (tracking the
whole guarded fetch as local work) would let time-to-headers and headers-to-first-event each take
a full budget, up to 2× the old ceiling, which is a weaker ceiling than before.
falsifying_evidence:
`watchdog-ceilings.test.ts` parks for 20,000 ms with a 1,000 ms first-event budget, then delivers headers after 600 ms and no body event.

- Bedrock, Google, Vertex Gemini, and Ollama abort at 1,000 ms after the wire.
- Anthropic, OpenAI completions, OpenAI responses, and Azure do not abort at 1,000 ms; first abort occurs at 1,600 ms. Each clears the pre-response guard at headers and gives its body iterator a fresh full first-event budget. All eventually time out; no never-ending provider stream was observed in this matrix.

lane_claim:
`CodexSteerPump` waits at the
hold twice — before it takes a message, so the message stays in the user's queue during a pause,
and again just before the send, because taking a message involves a wait a pause can land in — and
it hands a taken message back if the request is cancelled or the response ends while it waits, so
nothing is lost and no cancelled request parks forever.
falsifying_evidence:
```text
BOUNDARY_QUEUE_PAUSED { queue: 0, undelivered: 1, wire: [false] }
```

Normal resume works: a second request goes out unpaused. But cancelling the parked run produces:

```text
BOUNDARY_QUEUE_FINAL {
  ending: "abort", queue: 0, undelivered: 0, wire: [false],
  messages: [..., {role:"user",content:"queued task"},
                 {role:"assistant",content:[]}]
}
```

The boundary wait returns on abort and the loop commits its pending steering to history before noticing cancellation. It is no longer queued or undelivered, and no model request answered it.

lane_claim:
(b) Cursor HTTP/1
mid-turn appends (tool results) stay on the idle watchdog's clock: they share a path with the 5 s
heartbeats, and excluding them would let a stalled stream live forever.
falsifying_evidence:
```text
CURSOR_MIDTURN_HELD {
  appends: 1,
  holds: [false, false, false, true],
  paused: true,
  stopReason: "error",
  error: "Provider stream stalled while waiting for the next event"
}
0 pass / 1 fail
```

Only the initial append reached the wire. The completed tool's result did not. The server cannot answer because **we** withhold that result, yet the stream is killed as a provider stall.
